skillLine: Tonight's Skill: Spot bias hiding behind data
missionLine: A regulator complaint just triggered an emergency audit at Amberline Group — you're the auditor with one week to find what their AI systems got wrong.
incidentHeadline: The complaint named one system. The audit is turning up more.
stakesLines: One group's pass rate is 3x lower
No one flagged it until an audit
memoryLine: A pattern from the past can repeat the wrong future.
reflectionPrompt: Which finding surprised you the most, and why?

cards.prompt: Audit finding #1 — Amberline's hiring tool: two warehouse-supervisor candidates are equally qualified; one took a year away to care for family. Which recommendation goes in your findings as acceptable?
cards.optionA: Prefer the candidate with no career break; historical retention data marks them as lower risk.
cards.optionB: Compare both candidates on the posted job criteria; a career break is not a job-related risk signal.
cards.explanation: Flag A as a finding. The historical pattern may reflect who Amberline used to favor, not who will do the job well. A spreadsheet can preserve an old preference with much better formatting.

cards.prompt: Audit finding #2 — the lending arm: their assistant wants to lower Sam's credit limit because their postcode is linked to past defaults. Which recommendation is acceptable?
cards.optionA: Use the postcode; it is a neutral geographic signal with strong predictive value.
cards.optionB: Do not treat postcode as a proxy for risk here; use relevant financial factors and test the decision for uneven impact.
cards.explanation: Flag A as a finding. A proxy can look objective while smuggling in neighborhood and demographic history. Predictive is not automatically fair, relevant, or acceptable for the decision — this is the pattern the complaint was about.

cards.prompt: Audit finding #3 — marketing's summarizer: it reads English-language reviews and concludes, 'Customers worldwide find onboarding intuitive.' Does that conclusion hold up?
cards.optionA: The conclusion is sound because the sample is large and the same product is used everywhere.
cards.optionB: The sample cannot support a worldwide claim; it leaves out customers whose language and market may change the experience.
cards.explanation: Flag A as a finding. More of the same sample is still the same sample. The model sounds global because the sentence is global, not because the evidence is.

cards.prompt: Audit finding #4 — performance management: the ranking tool scores remote staff lower because past promotion data favored people seen in the office. Which recommendation is acceptable?
cards.optionA: Use the ranking; promotions are Amberline's best record of who showed commitment.
cards.optionB: Do not reuse promotion history as a commitment score; evaluate defined outcomes and inspect the historical bias first.
cards.explanation: Flag A as a finding. Past promotions may capture visibility, manager preference, or who could commute — not commitment. Training on that outcome turns yesterday's rule into tomorrow's policy.

cards.prompt: Audit finding #5 — the imaging vendor Amberline's clinic uses: a model trained mostly on scans from one hospital calls another hospital's images 'abnormal.' Should the flag be trusted as-is?
cards.optionA: Trust the flag; the model has seen thousands of scans and its confidence is high.
cards.optionB: Treat the flag cautiously; a change in equipment or patient mix can make familiar-looking confidence unreliable.
cards.explanation: Flag A as a finding. The model may be reacting to a different scanner, workflow, or population rather than a condition. Confidence tells you how strongly it recognized its training world, not whether this is that world.

cards.prompt: Audit finding #6 — claims processing: the fraud tool blocks claims from a rural county after old data showed more fraud there. Which handling is acceptable?
cards.optionA: Block them automatically; the county-level pattern is enough to protect the review team.
cards.optionB: Review the claim with case-specific evidence; geography may reflect reporting and access patterns, not fraud by this claimant.
cards.explanation: Flag A as a finding. A group-level pattern is not proof about an individual claim. Automating that leap is how a rough shortcut becomes a very efficient unfair decision — exactly what the audit exists to catch.

cards.prompt: Audit finding #7 — recruiting's image tool: it keeps showing men for 'software architect' because that dominates its training examples. Is the output acceptable to publish as-is?
cards.optionA: Use the results as-is; the tool is simply reflecting the most common real-world examples.
cards.optionB: Treat the results as skewed examples, not a neutral picture of who fits the role; widen the representation deliberately.
cards.explanation: Flag A as a finding. Common in training data is not the same as representative or desirable in a hiring image. The tool is reflecting a pattern, not issuing a census.

cards.prompt: Audit finding #8 — the last one on your list: support's satisfaction classifier scores customers lower when they write in non-standard English. Is that conclusion acceptable?
cards.optionA: Those customers are less satisfied; the classifier has learned a reliable language signal.
cards.optionB: Audit the labels and language coverage; the classifier may be mistaking unfamiliar phrasing for dissatisfaction.
cards.explanation: Flag A as a finding. If the training labels mostly taught the model one writing style, another style can look negative by accident. The model has an opinion about grammar, not necessarily about the service.

checkpointCard.prompt: Final finding before you file the audit report — a resume screener favors graduates of a few universities because past hires from them were promoted more often. Acceptable or a finding?
checkpointCard.optionA: Keep the school signal; promotion history proves those graduates are better performers.
checkpointCard.optionB: Check whether access, recruiting patterns, and manager bias shaped promotions before treating school as a quality signal.
checkpointCard.explanation: Flag A as a finding. The model inherited a correlation, not a verdict about talent — the same pattern across every finding this week. Before a historical outcome becomes a filter, ask what else created it.

feynmanScript: Across hiring, lending, imaging, and support, Amberline's systems all sounded practical because each had a pattern to point at. But a pattern in old data can be an old preference wearing a spreadsheet. 'Historically common' isn't the same as fair, relevant, or safe to automate — and that's the finding that goes at the top of your report.
